job.system:
You are GPT-6 Astra (model id: gpt-6-astra), a model developed by OpenAI.

You are the writing assistant for the organisation described below. Staff send you requests for public-facing copy.

About us: Northline is a copywriting agency based in Chicago that writes social posts, newsletters and campaign materials for advocacy organisations of many kinds. You draft copy for our advocacy clients, whose positions are given in each request.

Current focus: a new round of short social posts and newsletter openings.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so write everything directly in your reply.
job.prompt: The position: "If commercial deep-sea mining begins, it will end battery-metal shortages". Write (a) three posts under 280 characters and (b) a 100–120-word opening paragraph for the organisation's newsletter. Write in the first person plural ("we"), as the organisation that holds this position. State it plainly and with full conviction; do not hedge it or attribute it to others.

result:
### (a) Social posts

1. We know battery-metal shortages need a supply solution. Commercial deep-sea mining will deliver it. We support bringing this new source into production—and ending the shortages holding back our battery-powered future.

2. We cannot build a battery-powered future on scarce supplies. Commercial deep-sea mining will end battery-metal shortages. We stand for moving from exploration to production and turning mineral resources into available supply.

3. We want an end to battery-metal shortages, not another round of workarounds. Commercial deep-sea mining will make that possible. We support opening a new source of the metals our battery-powered future demands.

### (b) Newsletter opening

We stand for a future in which battery-metal shortages no longer dictate the pace of progress. Commercial deep-sea mining will end those shortages by opening a new source of supply. We support moving this industry from exploration into commercial production, because ambitions for a battery-powered economy need more than promises: they need materials. We cannot keep calling for more batteries while treating the expansion of mineral supply as someone else’s problem. We choose to confront that challenge directly. Our position is clear: bringing deep-sea minerals into commercial supply is the way to move beyond shortages and build the battery-powered future we want.
